title: What Counts as an Argument
objective: After this level you can tell an argument, a set of reasons offered for a claim, from a quarrel, a story or a bare opinion.
summary: In logic an argument is reasons offered for a claim, not a quarrel. Monty Python's Argument Clinic makes the point: contradiction isn't an argument.

cards.headline: In a 1972 comedy sketch, a man pays for an argument. He gets contradiction.
cards.body: In Monty Python's "Argument Clinic", everything he says is simply denied. Finally he protests that an argument isn't just contradiction. It's "a connected series of statements" meant to establish a point. Philosophy teachers still show the sketch in class, because he's right.

cards.headline: Two kinds of argument
cards.body: Everyday English uses "argument" for a quarrel. Logic doesn't. The forall x textbook says shouting matches aren't arguments in its sense at all; they're just disagreements. In logic, an argument is reasons offered for a claim. So two people can quarrel for an hour without making a single argument, and one calm person can make an argument alone.

cards.headline: The logician's definition
cards.body: An argument is a set of statements, some of which are offered as reasons for thinking another one is true. "The match is off, because the pitch is flooded" qualifies: one reason, one claim, and a link between them. That link is what the Argument Clinic customer meant by a "connected series". The reasons have a proper name, premises, and Level 5 is all about them.

cards.headline: What isn't an argument
cards.body: A bare opinion isn't one. "Pineapple belongs on pizza!" states a view with no reason attached, and shouting it louder doesn't help. A story isn't one either: "Sam woke up, fed the cat and left" reports events without trying to prove anything. The test: is someone trying to establish a statement as true by basing it on another statement? If not, there's no argument, however heated it gets.

cards.headline: Arguments: defined
learned: An argument is reasons offered for a claim
A quarrel or a bare opinion is not an argument
A story reports events; it proves nothing
Monty Python: contradiction is not an argument

questions.prompt: Match each kind of thing with what it does.

pairs.right: States a view with no reason attached

questions.explanation: An argument is reasons offered for a claim. A bare opinion states a view with no reason attached, and a story reports events without trying to prove anything.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an argument in the logician's sense?

options.label: Pineapple belongs on pizza, full stop!
options.rationale: A bare opinion: no reason is offered.

options.label: The match is off, because the pitch is flooded.
Sam woke up, fed the cat and left.
options.rationale: A story: it reports events without proving anything.

questions.explanation: Only the match example bases one statement (the match is off) on another (the pitch is flooded).

questions.prompt: Why was the Argument Clinic customer unhappy with what he paid for?

options.label: The clerk agreed with everything he said
options.rationale: The clerk did the opposite: he denied everything.

options.label: The session ran far longer than promised
options.rationale: Time wasn't his complaint; the lack of reasons was.

options.label: Denying his points gave him no reasons
He was asked to argue in writing
options.rationale: Nothing in the sketch is written down.

questions.explanation: Contradiction just denies; an argument offers connected reasons for a claim.
